stops.name: The road to Gniezno: barefoot to Adalbert's tomb
stops.campa: In deep winter Otto leaves Rome in secret, telling almost no one his destination, and travels north and east, through Regensburg, through the March of Meissen, on a pilgrimage of debt: to the grave of Adalbert, his friend and confessor, murdered on the Baltic shore three years before. Nearing Gniezno he dismounts and walks the last distance on foot, then barefoot in the snow, as the poorest pilgrims do, and comes so into the church holding Adalbert's relics, weeping, to pray at the tomb before the assembled clergy and Duke Bolesław's court, who watch their emperor arrive like a penitent, not a conqueror.

stops.name: Gniezno: the Congress, the diadem, and Poland's church
stops.campa: For a week emperor and duke feast and confer as equals. Otto lifts the imperial diadem from his own head and sets it on Bolesław's, naming him *frater et cooperator imperii*, brother and partner of the empire, and friend of the Roman people; in exchange he receives a relic arm of Saint Adalbert and gives a copy of the Holy Lance. Before they part, Otto raises Gniezno to an archbishopric with three suffragan sees, founding the independent church of Poland at a stroke. Bolesław, at the banquet's end, gathers every gold and silver vessel used at table and presses it on the emperor as tribute of honor.
stops.quote: [Otto III] took the imperial diadem from his own head and laid it upon the head of Bolesław in pledge of friendship.
stops.quote_source: Gallus Anonymus, Gesta principum Polonorum I.6

stops.name: Aachen: Otto III opens the vault in the year 1000
stops.campa: At Pentecost of the millennial year Emperor Otto III has the pavement of the chapel broken and goes down with Count Otto of Lomello into the vault. They find him as the register promised: not lying as the dead lie, but seated on a throne as if alive, the golden crown on the skull, the sceptre in gloved hands, and the fingernails, grown on in death, have pierced through the gloves. Nothing has fallen away but the tip of the nose, which Otto restores in gold. He clothes the dead emperor in white, cuts the nails, takes one tooth for a relic, and seals the tomb.
stops.quote: He was not lying, as the bodies of other dead men lie, but sat upon a throne as though living, crowned with a golden crown, holding a sceptre in gloved hands, through which his fingernails had grown and pierced.
stops.quote_source: Chronicon Novaliciense III.32 (the account of Count Otto of Lomello)

stops.name: Rome: the revolt, the tower speech, and exile
stops.campa: The peace does not survive the year. When Otto pardons the rebellious town of Tivoli instead of levelling it as the Romans demand, the city turns on its own emperor in February, storms his palace, and traps him inside for three days. From a tower he makes the speech Rome will remember longest: he calls them still his Romans, says he abandoned Saxony and all his own blood for their sake, led them to a greatness their fathers never reached. It does not move them. He slips out by night and rides for Ravenna, exiled from the very city he built to be eternal.
stops.quote: Are you not my Romans? For your sake I left my homeland and my kinsmen; for the love of you I have rejected my Saxons and all Germans, my own blood.
stops.quote_source: Thangmar, Vita Bernwardi c. 25 (the address from the tower, Rome 1001)

stops.name: Paterno: the fever and the death of the emperor
stops.campa: Otto spends the rest of the year gathering an army to retake Rome by force, but at Paterno, a hill-fort north of the city near Civita Castellana, a fever, malaria, most likely, the old curse of Roman campaigns, takes hold in January and will not let go. Around his bed stand Pope Sylvester, his chancellor Heribert of Cologne, and his cousin Duke Henry of Bavaria. He dies on the twenty-third or twenty-fourth of January, twenty-one years old, unmarried, without an heir of his body: the Ottonian line's whole hope narrowed in an instant to a cousin's ambition and a boy's empty throne.

stops.name: The road north to Verona: the winter cortège
stops.campa: His household will not leave him among the Romans who hated him living. They arm the body's escort as though for battle, ride out of Paterno by night, and fight their way north through a countryside that curses the corpse as it passes: stones thrown, ambushes attempted, the dead emperor's cortège shadowed the whole road by men hoping to seize the imperial insignia carried with it. They reach the safety of Verona on the seventh of February, past the worst of hostile Italy at last, while behind them in Pavia the Lombard nobles are already crowning a rival, Arduin of Ivrea, before Otto is even buried.

stops.name: Aachen: burial beside Charlemagne, Easter 1002
stops.campa: The cortège crosses the Alps and the length of Germany through the late winter, gathering the mourning and the ambitious both, until on Easter Sunday it reaches Aachen, the city of the boyhood coronation, the city of the opened tomb not two years past. They bury Otto before the altar of Our Lady, close by Charlemagne's own resting place, the two emperors of the Renovatio now neighbors in the same choir. He came to the throne asleep in someone's arms and leaves it the same way. Within months the German crown will pass, after a hard election, to his cousin Henry.
